read: full: abstract, sections 1-5, appendices A.1-A.3 (semi-automated verification, generation details, grading prompts in Table 5, human check of the grader in Table 6); worked examples in A.2 and A.4 skimmed
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2410.09988v2, 13 Dec 2024, headed 'A PREPRINT' (p1); the text shows no venue
what_it_is: HARDMath is a set of graduate-level applied-mathematics problems that need asymptotic and approximation methods (nondimensionalisation, polynomial roots and correction terms, nonlinear third-order ODEs, traditional and Laplace integrals), inspired by a Harvard graduate course (p1, p3-6). Problems and step-by-step solutions are generated by SymPy/SciPy code from random coefficients, functional forms and initial conditions, and a problem is kept only if its approximation is within 10% of a numerical ground truth (p2, p4-5). It has a 1,060-problem development set, the 366-problem HARDMath-Mini evaluation set and 40 hand-written word problems in applied contexts (p1, p4, p6). Scoring combines automatic boxed-answer checks with GPT-4o as a rubric-driven 'procedural grader' that gives partial credit (p7).
domain: graduate applied mathematics (asymptotic analysis); 40 word problems set in applied science contexts
size: 1,466 problems: 1,060 development, 366 HARDMath-Mini, 40 word problems (p1, p4, p10); five models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, o1-mini, Llama3-8b, CodeLlama-13b) at 0, 1 and 5 shots (p7-8)
source_of_items: generated from code (SymPy/SciPy algorithms per problem type) (p2, p4); 40 word problems hand-written (p4, p6); a preliminary LLM pipeline that writes physics contexts for 30 generated ODE problems (p6)
instances: generated: the code 'can be used to generate any number of additional problems' (p2); the released evaluation set is fixed at 366
has_gold_traces: yes: algorithmically generated step-by-step solutions, each step embedded in explanatory text, with boxed results (p4) and a comparison against a numerical ground truth for every problem (p5)
evaluation: final answer plus LLM judge: boxed answers checked by SymPy equivalence and numerical evaluation; GPT-4o as a 'procedural grader' given the answer key and course-derived rubrics, with partial credit, for Roots, ODEs and Integrals (p7). The rubrics (Table 5, p25) mostly score each regime's final expression; only the Laplace-integral rubric credits an intermediate checkpoint (half credit for finding t0 and attempting the Taylor expansion).
human_validation: Items: kept only if within 10% of the numerical ground truth (automatic); HARDMath-Mini checked by plotting analytical against numerical solutions, a 'semi-automated' visual human check (p5, p13); manual step-by-step verification is called impractical (p5). Grader: 'We manually verify a subset of grading responses and found that LLM-based grading is closely aligned with human grading' (p7); Table 6 gives average score adjustments per model and problem type from -0.15 to +0.07 (p26); no subset size or agreement statistic is given.
contamination_measures: generated instances (any number of new problems can be generated, p2); no contamination analysis; code and data are public on GitHub (p1)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-M1 (L155-161): '... benchmarks ranging from GSM8K ... and Math ... to HardMath (Fan et al., 2024), Putnam-Axiom ..., and GSM-Symbolic ... rigorously test abstract logical deduction and reasoning stability.'
engtrace_use.explanation: HARDMath defines itself against what the sentence says it tests. It faults other hard datasets for focusing 'on abstract, formal mathematics' (p2) and earlier datasets for problems solved by direct, clean calculations (p2), and it targets approximate analytical solutions to problems 'commonly encountered in real-world scientific and engineering contexts' (p1), which demand 'a combination of mathematical reasoning, computational tools, and subjective judgment' (p1). It does not test reasoning stability. S-M3 then uses the group as the example of abstract skill that does not transfer to physical constraints, which HARDMath's applied framing and its 40 applied word problems (p1, p6, p8) do not fit. The sentence also omits what matters most for the comparison: HARDMath generates problems and step-by-step solutions in code (p2, p4), validates every solution against a numerical ground truth (p5), and grades intermediate work with a rubric-driven LLM grader (p7). That makes it a close precedent for EngTrace's generated instances with gold solutions, and a counterexample to the closing claim that existing benchmarks 'remain limited to outcome matching' (S-E3).

suggested_wording: HARDMath (Fan et al., 2024) generates graduate-level applied-mathematics problems and step-by-step solutions in code, keeps those whose approximations fall within 10% of a numerical ground truth, and adds a rubric-driven LLM grader for partial credit to its final-answer checks.
facts_to_cite: 1,466 problems inspired by a graduate course on asymptotic methods: a 1,060-problem development set, the 366-problem HARDMath-Mini evaluation set and 40 hand-written word problems (p1, p4, p10).

Problems and step-by-step solutions are generated with SymPy and SciPy from randomly selected coefficients, functional forms and initial conditions, with no duplicates (p2, p4); the code 'can be used to generate any number of additional problems' (p2).

A problem is included only if its approximate solution is within 10% of the numerically computed ground truth (p5); HARDMath-Mini is checked by plotting analytical against numerical solutions (p5, p13).
Scoring combines boxed-answer checks (SymPy equivalence and numerical evaluation) with GPT-4o as a 'procedural grader' given the answer key and course-derived rubrics (p7).
The authors report manually checking a subset of the GPT-4o grades and list average score adjustments (Table 6, p26), but give no agreement statistic (p7).
Best accuracy on HARDMath-Mini: o1-mini 62.3% with 5-shot CoT; GPT-4 43.8% (p7; Table 2, p8).
The authors position HARDMath against 'abstract, formal mathematics' (p2) and towards approximations needed in 'real-world scientific and engineering contexts' (p1).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: generated instances from code with a code-generated step-by-step solution for each (p2, p4), i.e. generated gold traces; numerical validation of every generated solution (p5), comparable to EngTrace's deterministic Layer 0 gate; partial credit; an LLM grader with rubrics (p7); applied, engineering-adjacent mathematics (p1). Lacks: engineering domain proper (it is mathematics, with 40 word problems); step-level verification of model traces (the rubrics score per-regime final expressions, with one checkpoint for Laplace integrals, p25); expert validation of the evaluator with an agreement statistic (only an unsized subset checked, p7); a private pool (code and data public, p1).
notes: In Batch M this is the closest methodological precedent to EngTrace, closer than GSM-Symbolic: generated problems with generated step-by-step solutions, each validated numerically. It deserves the credit S-I2 gives to symbolic templates, alongside GSM-Symbolic and Putnam-AXIOM's variants. The May text writes 'HardMath'; the paper writes HARDMath. The text is arXiv v2 ('A PREPRINT') and shows no venue; the May entry cites the same arXiv id, and the consolidator may want to check whether a published version exists.
